title: Paper 1 Section C World Religions Guide
summary: Paper 1 Section C world religions guide to Taoism, Jainism and the Baha'i Faith, with smart timing, stimulus technique and a concise worked example for exams.
body_markdown:
Paper 1 rewards a skill that can feel strange at first: saying something precise before saying everything you know. For IB World Religions SL students, that distinction matters. A response can contain accurate religious knowledge and still lose marks if it does not interpret the stimulus or answer the command directly.


This paper 1 section c world religions guide focuses on Taoism, Jainism and the Baha'i Faith. You will learn the exam format, the concepts worth connecting, and a practical method for handling both parts of each stimulus question.


### Paper 1 format at a glance


Paper 1 lasts **1 hour 15 minutes** . You answer **five stimulus-based questions** , selecting at least one question from each of the paper's three sections. Section C contains questions on **Taoism, Jainism and the Baha'i Faith** .


Each selected question is worth 10 marks:


Part Marks Main task


Part (a) 3 Demonstrate focused knowledge and understanding of an idea connected to the stimulus


Part (b) 7 Develop an explained response using the stimulus and relevant religious knowledge


Five questions in 75 minutes gives you an average of **15 minutes per question** . A sensible starting structure is approximately four minutes for part (a), ten minutes for part (b), and one minute to check whether you answered the command.


Before writing, remember this checklist:


- Identify the religion and central concept in the stimulus.
- Underline the command term and limiting words.
- Give part (a) a direct definition plus relevant detail.
- Build part (b) around explained connections, not a list of facts.
- Refer to the stimulus explicitly.
- Use accurate terminology and explain what each term means.
- Move on when your allocated time ends.


For wider preparation, the[IB World Religions mock exam guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-world-religions-mock-exam-prep-november) offers a structured approach to recall, writing practice and timed review.


### What Section C is really testing


The stimulus might be a short passage, image or other source linked to a religious idea. It is not there as decoration. It gives you the doorway through which your knowledge must pass.


Part (a) normally rewards concise knowledge and understanding. If asked about *wu wei* , for example, naming it as “doing nothing” would be misleading. A stronger answer explains it as unforced or non-coercive action aligned with the Dao, then adds a consequence or application.


Part (b) asks for development. That means showing how and why ideas connect. A useful paragraph pattern is:


**Claim → religious concept → explanation → stimulus link → significance**


Imagine the stimulus presents simplicity as a path towards harmony. A weak answer merely lists the Dao, *wu wei* , *yin and yang* , and *ziran* . A stronger answer explains how simplicity reduces artificial desire, allowing action to become less forced and more aligned with the natural Way.


One student carries an enormous stack of books while another asks whether it contains an answer to the question


Knowledge matters. Selection matters just as much.


### Taoism: connect harmony, action and transformation


Taoism questions the assumption that more effort always produces better results. The **Dao** can be understood as the Way or underlying course through which reality unfolds. Because the Dao cannot be reduced to a simple human formula, Taoist wisdom involves receptiveness, humility and sensitivity to natural patterns.


Several concepts form a useful network:


- **Wu wei:** unforced action that does not impose artificial control.
- **Ziran:** naturalness or spontaneity, often understood as being so of itself.
- **Yin and yang:** interdependent tendencies whose changing relationship expresses balance and transformation.
- **De:** virtue, potency or integrity expressed by living in accordance with the Dao.
- **Qi:** vital energy associated with life and the dynamic processes of existence.


Do not treat these as isolated definitions. If a stimulus describes a ruler who governs without constant interference, connect *wu wei* to leadership. If it presents water, flexibility or yielding, explain how apparent weakness can express effectiveness without aggression.


Avoid claiming that Taoism requires complete passivity. The point is not that a Taoist never acts. It is that wise action works with conditions instead of forcing reality into an artificial pattern.


### Jainism: trace the movement from karma to liberation


Jainism offers a highly disciplined account of the human condition. Living beings possess **jiva** , or soul, but karmic matter binds the soul within the cycle of rebirth. Liberation requires stopping new karmic influx and removing accumulated karma through ethical conduct, knowledge and discipline.


For Paper 1 stimulus questions, learn the relationships among these ideas:


- **Ahimsa:** non-violence towards living beings in thought, speech and action.
- **Karma:** a form of matter that binds the soul rather than only a system of moral reward.
- **The Three Jewels:** right faith, right knowledge and right conduct.
- **Aparigraha:** non-attachment or non-possession.
- **Anekantavada:** the many-sided nature of reality and the limits of any single viewpoint.
- **Moksha:** liberation of the soul from karma and rebirth.


A stimulus about diet, careful movement or restraint should not produce a paragraph that stops at “Jains avoid harm.” Explain the spiritual logic. Harm attracts karma, karma obstructs the soul, and disciplined non-violence supports purification and eventual liberation.


Distinctions also earn clarity. Jain ascetics and lay Jains may observe vows at different levels of strictness. A careful answer therefore avoids presenting every Jain practice as identical for every believer.


### The Baha'i Faith: link revelation with unity


The Baha'i Faith understands religious history through **progressive revelation** . God is ultimately beyond complete human comprehension, but divine guidance is communicated through Manifestations of God at different stages of humanity's development.


This helps connect several central themes:


- **The oneness of God:** religions share one divine source.
- **The oneness of religion:** major religions belong to an unfolding process of revelation.
- **The oneness of humanity:** humanity forms one family despite cultural diversity.
- **Manifestations of God:** figures who bring divine teachings suited to particular historical conditions.
- **Baha'u'llah:** the founder of the Baha'i Faith and the Manifestation associated with the present age.
- **Service and consultation:** practical expressions of unity and collective responsibility.


If a stimulus discusses religious diversity, do not merely say that the Baha'i Faith respects other religions. Explain why: progressive revelation interprets their teachings as stages in one divine educational process. Differences can reflect changing human needs rather than competing divine sources.


Students sometimes confuse unity with uniformity. The principle of human oneness does not require every culture to become identical. A stronger explanation presents diversity and unity as compatible.


The[IB World Religions misconceptions guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-world-religions-misconceptions) can help you correct broad assumptions before they enter an exam response. The[first-term World Religions overview](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/first-term-ib-world-religions) also explains how the course's fundamental questions connect beliefs, practices and lived experience.


### A short worked example


Consider this invented Taoist practice stimulus:


> A wise person responds to changing circumstances without forcing a predetermined result.


**Part (a), 3 marks:** Explain the meaning of *wu wei* .


A focused response could state that *wu wei* means unforced or non-coercive action aligned with the Dao. It does not require literal inactivity. Instead, a person acts responsively and avoids imposing excessive control against the natural course of events.


**Part (b), 7 marks:** Explain how the stimulus reflects Taoist ideas about living well.


A strong response could begin by connecting “changing circumstances” to the Taoist understanding of reality as dynamic. It would then explain that attachment to a predetermined outcome can produce artificial and forceful action. Through *wu wei* , the wise person responds to conditions rather than struggling against them. The answer could add that *ziran* supports naturalness and spontaneity, while yin and yang illustrate continual transformation. Finally, it should return to the stimulus and explain that living well means adapting with humility, not controlling every outcome.


Notice what this approach does not do. It does not recite every Taoist term available. It chooses concepts that help answer this particular question.


### How to revise for the IB World Religions exam


Build revision around connections rather than enormous topic summaries. For each religion, create a one-page map linking the human condition, ultimate goal, central teachings, ethical practices and community life.


Then turn those links into retrieval questions. RevisionDojo's **Flashcards** can test definitions, while the **Questionbank** lets you practise moving from recall to application. Use **Study Notes** to repair gaps, and ask **Jojo AI Chat** to challenge a vague explanation or generate a contrasting stimulus.


Writing still needs feedback. Submit practice responses to RevisionDojo's **AI Grading tools** , compare your structure with the **Coursework Library** , and use **Predicted Papers** or **Mock Exams** for timed rehearsal. A **Tutor** can be especially useful when your knowledge is sound but your seven-mark answers remain descriptive.


The broader[ultimate IB revision guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-revision-for-ib-students) explains how retrieval, spacing and timed practice can work together. You can also browse the[IB World Religions resource collection](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/tag/ib-world-religions) when you need topic-specific guidance.


### Make precision your advantage


Paper 1 does not reward the student who carries the largest pile of disconnected information into the room. It rewards the student who notices what the stimulus is doing, selects the right knowledge, and explains the relationship clearly.


Know the concepts. Practise the links. Respect the 15-minute limit. With RevisionDojo's Questionbank, Study Notes, Flashcards, grading support and realistic Mock Exams, Section C becomes less like a memory contest and more like what it was designed to be: a test of informed religious understanding.
